title: Short Stuff: Candy Corn
summary: Halloween-themed Short Stuff episode on candy corn. Josh and Chuck open with banter about the "spoopy" bit and their feelings toward candy corn. They cover its origins in the 1880s, the murky credit given to George Renninger, a candy designer at the Wonderly Candy Company in Philadelphia, and its predecessors like mellow cream candies. They explain that corn was then mostly chicken feed, that Goelitz (spelled "Golitz" in the transcript) sold it to kids, and that candy corn became linked to Halloween in the mid-twentieth century. They describe traditional manufacturing (kettles, runners, corn-starch molds, stringers pouring in three passes of white, yellow, orange), the modern ingredients, and production figures from the National Confectioners Association. They close with survey and popularity stats: National Retail Federation Halloween shopping data, candystore.com state rankings and a poll of 3,247 people (56% fans, 44% not), and how people eat it.

segments.title: Spooky banter and candy corn opinions
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Halloween-themed episode with banter about the word 'spoopy' and share their feelings about candy corn, with Josh disliking it and Chuck feeling only nostalgia.

segments.title: Origins and George Renninger
segments.summary: Candy corn dates to around the 1880s, though its origins are murky. Its predecessors were mellow cream candies, including shaped vegetables. Credit for invention goes to George Renninger, a candy designer at the Wonderly Candy Company in Philadelphia.

segments.title: Chicken feed candy and early marketing
segments.summary: Candy corn was first sold year round, not as a Halloween candy, and was meant to look like corn kernels, which were then mostly chicken feed. Goelitz sold it to kids and exposed it to the public. Candy corn became linked to Halloween in the mid-twentieth century as corn became a common food.

segments.title: Corn preferences tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck briefly discuss how they feel about eating corn.

segments.title: Break and manufacturing history
segments.summary: After a break, Chuck describes the traditional process: sugar and corn syrup cooked in kettles, poured into runners, and stringers pouring the slurry into corn-starch molds in three color passes, with the stringers walking backwards.

segments.title: Modern ingredients and production
segments.summary: Modern candy corn is still made of sugar water, corn syrup, vanilla flavoring, and marshmallow cream, poured into corn-starch molds. The National Confectioners Association says about 35 million pounds, or nine billion pieces, are produced annually.

segments.title: Candy corn crafts and Halloween shopping
segments.summary: Candy corn's fall colors make it popular for crafts. The National Retail Federation found that in 2019, 95 percent of Halloween shoppers bought candy corn.

segments.title: Popularity survey and how people eat it
segments.summary: candystore.com's shipping data put candy corn in the top three candies in many states and eighth nationally. Its poll of 3,247 people found 56 percent fans and 44 percent not. Reasons include nostalgia and sweetness, and people eat it in different ways.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the episode, noting that Halloween is near and that Short Stuff is out, followed by the production credit.
